strengths: The paper tackles a clearly motivated and under-explored problem: structurally and dynamically updating ViT architectures during exemplar-free task-incremental continual learning, in contrast to prior prompt-based or fixed parameter-tuning approaches.

The core idea of localizing the task-synergy memory at the output projection layer after MHSA is supported by a systematic empirical study (Table 1) comparing 11 candidate components in terms of transferability and forgetting, rather than being asserted.

The proposed HEE sampling (hierarchical exploration-exploitation) over Reuse/Adapt/New/Skip operations is well-motivated and convincingly validated: Table 4 and Fig. 7 show a ~6-7% absolute accuracy gain over uniform (pure exploration) sampling, and the HEE advantage is stable across 5 different task orders (Table 13), a substantial and often-neglected robustness check.

Experiments are thorough: results on VDD and 5-Datasets, two learning protocols (sequential continual and task-to-task transfer), comparison against multiple strong baselines (L2G with DARTS/beta-DARTS adapted to ViTs, L2P, S-Prompts, SupSup, EFT, LL, EWC, L2-replay), 3 seeds with error bars, and parameter/FLOPs accounting.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on VDD (83.44 vs 80.08 for the best prompt baseline) and 5-Datasets (94.82), with the claimed 'sensible' learned task synergies (Fig. 4, Fig. 10) showing reasonable reuse of similar-task components.

Strong reproducibility effort: PyTorch code is provided, detailed hyperparameters are given, baselines are carefully re-implemented/modified for ViTs and VDD (Appendix F), and ablations cover memory location (Table 11) and Adapt implementation (Table 12).
weaknesses: The task-incremental setting requires task IDs at test time, which substantially limits practical relevance compared to class-incremental settings; the paper acknowledges this (Sec. 3.3) but only sketches potential solutions without results.

Potential unfairness in compute/epoch comparisons: CHEEM uses 100 supernet epochs + 30 finetuning epochs per task, while L2G uses 50/30 and prompt-based baselines receive no task-specific backbone training; the prompt baselines (0.01M params/task) are far cheaper in parameters, whereas CHEEM adds ~1.06M params/task — the efficiency claims are mixed and somewhat selectively framed (FLOPs favored, parameters not).

The 'sweet spot' claim is weakened by the paper's own ablations: the FFN location achieves the best accuracy (84.20 in Table 1, 84.20 in Table 11) and is only rejected on parameter-cost grounds; a strict accuracy-vs-cost analysis of all 11 components would make the identification more convincing.

The task-similarity heuristic based on mean CLS tokens (Eqs. 4-5) is central to the method but receives little analysis or justification; the min-max normalization of cosine similarity and the auxiliary expert score appear to be empirically tuned design choices rather than principled ones.

CHEEM's per-task supernet training, evolutionary search, and retraining-from-scratch of new layers adds significant per-task computational overhead relative to prompt-style methods, and total parameter growth is unbounded as tasks accumulate, with no analysis of scalability to long task streams.

The improvement over the strongest task-to-task baseline (LL, 83.10 -> 84.65) is more modest than over the sequential-continual baselines, and the method behaves differently across the two protocols (Fig. 13 vs Fig. 4), suggesting some sensitivity of the NAS-based approach to the training regime.

Presentation issues remain: several typos ('Tabe 3', 'feature work', 'one-short' in the conclusion), Table 1 lacks forgetting-standard-error details, and the contribution claims in the introduction are somewhat inflated given that the framework is an extension of L2G to ViTs with a new search strategy.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: structurally and dynamically updating Vision Transformer architectures in task-incremental continual learning, and claims to be the first to evaluate ViT-based continual learning on the challenging, diverse and imbalanced VDD benchmark.

Empirical results are strong and reasonably thorough: CHEEM outperforms adapted prior art (L2G with DARTS/beta-DARTS, L2P, S-Prompts) by ~3.3% on VDD and beats SupSup, EFT and LL under the task-to-task protocol, with results averaged over 3 seeds and 5 task orders for the 5-Datasets benchmark.

The ablation studies are extensive and mostly convincing: the HEE sampling vs. pure exploration comparison (Table 4, Fig. 7) shows a large ~6% gap and better parameter efficiency; the task-order ablations (Table 13) show robustness of the gains; the component-choice ablation (Tables 1 and 11) supports the choice of the MHSA output projection as the 'sweet spot'; the Adapt-shortcut ablation (Table 12) is a useful design analysis.

The efficiency analysis is candid: parameter growth (1.06M/task) and FLOPs growth (0.17G/task) are reported and contextualized against L2P, and the learned structures across seeds (Figs. 10-11) demonstrate stability of the discovered task synergies.
The authors put considerable effort into materializing baselines for ViTs (modifying L2G, L2P, S-Prompts, SupSup, EFT, LL) and release code and baseline implementations, which aids reproducibility.
Limitations are honestly stated, including the task-ID assumption at inference and the difficulty of extending to class-incremental learning on VDD.
weaknesses: The task-incremental setting is a relatively weak and increasingly less-favored setting: task IDs are assumed available at both training and inference, and no forgetting occurs by construction within CHEEM (task-specific experts are frozen once learned). This weakens the 'catastrophic forgetting overcome' framing; the paper largely sidesteps the core difficulty of continual learning rather than solving it, and no CCL experiments are provided despite acknowledging that CCL has attracted much more attention.

Novelty is incremental relative to Learning-to-Grow (L2G). The paper itself admits CHEEM is 'motivated by the L2G method.' The core contributions reduce to (i) applying L2G-style structural search to the MHSA output projection of a ViT, and (ii) replacing uniform/DARTS sampling with a heuristic similarity-based hierarchical sampling using pooled CLS-token cosine similarity. These are sensible but largely engineering refinements; several hand-crafted components (normalized min-max cosine similarity, the Aux expert with score -max(S), sigmoid-based Bernoulli rates, epoch-wise epsilon scheduling) are heuristic patches whose individual necessity is not dissected.

Comparison fairness concerns: CHEEM trains the supernet for 100 epochs plus 30 epochs of finetuning while the strongest baselines (SupSup, EFT, LL) use 50 epochs; the accuracy gap could partially reflect training-budget differences. Additionally, baselines were re-implemented/modified by the authors rather than using published numbers, and results are reported on the official validation set (no test labels available), which inflates comparability uncertainty.

The component-selection ablation (Table 1) is performed under plain sequential fine-tuning without any forgetting-mitigation mechanism, which is a rather crude instrument for identifying a 'sweet spot'; the differences between Projection (85.11) and alternatives like MHSA+LN1 (85.26) or FFN (84.20) are small and the choice is partly justified post hoc by simplicity.

Cost and complexity of the method are non-trivial: per-task supernet training + evolutionary search + retraining is expensive, and the extra parameters (1.06M/task) dwarf prompt-based methods (0.01M/task); the 'new FLOPs' of some learned models are negative (e.g., -2.657M, -0.429G in Fig. 4), which is confusing and suggests the efficiency reporting needs clearer definitions. Scalability to long task streams (unbounded expert growth, Adapt-on-Adapt stacking) is not convincingly demonstrated.

Presentation issues: numerous typos ('shortchut', 'finetuing', 'one-short', 'feature work'), negative parameter/FLOPs entries without explanation, and Fig. 4 is nearly unreadable without magnification. The paper also cites the L2P parameter cost against 'Li et al., 2019' in one place, a citation error.

The main empirical story rests on a single backbone (ViT-B/8) and one pretrained initialization recipe; no results with other ViT scales or patch sizes, and no comparison with natural PEFT competitors (adapters, VPT, LoRA-style task modules with task-ID routing) that would seem to be the most obvious strong baselines for the TCL setting.

strengths: The paper tackles a meaningful and under-explored problem: structurally and dynamically updating Vision Transformer architectures in task-incremental continual learning, extending the learning-to-grow paradigm (Li et al., 2019) from ConvNets to ViTs. The claim of being the first to evaluate ViT-based continual learning on the large-scale, diverse, and imbalanced VDD benchmark is plausible and adds benchmark value to the community.

The method is technically well-conceived. The identification of the MHSA output projection layer as the task-synergy 'sweet spot' is supported by a systematic component-wise ablation (Table 1 and Appendix E.1, Table 11), trading off forward transferability against forgetting. The Mixture-of-Experts formulation with Reuse/Adapt/New/Skip operations is clean, and the HEE sampling strategy driven by normalized cosine similarity of pooled task-specific CLS tokens is a sensible exploitation mechanism within SPOS-style NAS.

The empirical evidence is convincing. CHEEM achieves 83.44% average accuracy on VDD vs. 80.08% (L2P), 80.00% (S-Prompts), and ~77-78% (L2G with DARTS/beta-DARTS) in the sequential continual learning setting (Table 2), and 84.65% vs. 83.10% (LL), 82.60% (EFT), 81.14% (SupSup) in the task-to-task transfer setting (Table 5), with consistent gains across 3 seeds and 5 task orders (Appendix E.3, Table 13). The 5-Datasets benchmark result (94.82%) also outperforms prior art.

The ablation of pure exploration (PE) vs. proposed HEE sampling (Table 4: 76.45% vs. 83.44%, and Fig. 7 showing HEE with 50 epochs beats PE with 300 epochs) clearly isolates the contribution of the proposed sampling strategy rather than only of architectural search itself.

The efficiency analysis is appreciable: despite larger per-task parameter growth than prompt methods (1.06M/task), CHEEM adds only 0.17G FLOPs/task, roughly 10x less than L2P, and the appendix carefully dissects the Adapt-operation shortcut design trade-off (Table 12), including the honest choice of the more parameter-efficient variant even though the shortcut variant performs better.

Reproducibility is strong: code is provided, hyperparameters, data splits, data augmentations, and the non-trivial baseline modifications (Appendix F) are documented in detail, and the appendix includes learned-structure visualizations across seeds and task orders supporting stability of the learned synergies.
weaknesses: The setting is task-incremental, requiring task IDs at both training and inference. While the authors candidly acknowledge this limitation (Sec. 3.3) and justify it by inapplicability of most CCL methods to VDD's varying label spaces, this limits practical relevance relative to the more active class-incremental literature, and the proposed remedy (task-index inference from mean CLS tokens) remains preliminary.

Novelty is incremental relative to Learning-to-Grow (Li et al., 2019), which already introduces reuse/adapt/new operations via NAS. The main advances are application to ViTs, the Skip operation, the projection-layer identification, and HEE sampling; the individual ingredients (SPOS, MoE-style experts, CLS-based similarity, residual adaptation) are largely borrowed, so the contribution rests heavily on the empirical synthesis.

Baseline comparability concerns: the L2P/S-Prompts baselines were re-implemented/modified for the VDD task-incremental setting (Appendix F.1), and training epochs differ across methods (CHEEM uses 100+30 epochs vs. 50 for L2G and baselines in Tables 2/5). The identical 82.65% ImNet column across all methods in Tables 2, 3, 5 suggests a shared frozen first-task model, which is reasonable but warrants more explicit discussion of its effect on the comparison. The L2G-ResNet26 row is directly copied from prior work rather than re-run under identical conditions.

The evaluation protocol reports accuracy on the official validation set because official VDD test labels are unavailable (Appendix A.1). This is a known community-wide caveat, but it slightly weakens cross-paper comparability and should be flagged more prominently.

The task-similarity heuristic (Eqns. 4-5) is ad hoc: min-max normalization of cosine similarities across all experts, a hand-crafted Aux similarity score (Eqn. 5), and fixed exploration probabilities (epsilon1=0.3, epsilon2=0.5) are introduced without sensitivity analysis or theoretical justification. The method also carries considerable pipeline complexity (supernet training, evolutionary search, per-expert CLS token pooling), and the computational cost of the supernet/search phases relative to simpler alternatives is not quantified.

Some claims are overstated or inconsistently supported: Table 1 shows Projection (85.11/30.50) is statistically similar in accuracy to MHSA+LN1 (85.26) and the ablation in Appendix E.1 shows the FFN actually yields slightly higher average accuracy (84.20% vs. 83.44%), so the 'sweet spot' identification is defensible mainly on the forgetting/efficiency trade-off rather than accuracy. Minor editorial issues (e.g., 'L2P (Li et al., 2019)' citation error in the efficiency paragraph, 'Tabe 3', 'one-short' in the conclusion) detract from polish.

Experiments use ViT-B/8 at 72x72 resolution with a 2048-batch fine-tuning recipe from full-resolution ImageNet weights; the interaction between low input resolution and ViT behavior (and thus generalization of the 'sweet spot' finding to standard 224x224 settings) is not investigated, and only two benchmarks are evaluated, both with relatively small images for ViTs.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies underexplored design axes in exemplar-free class-incremental learning with ViTs (task-difficulty/synergy-aware computation, Skip and New operations), and positions its contribution against a well-organized taxonomy of prior art (Fig. 1).

The proposed CHEEM is technically coherent: a MoE-based internal parameter memory with four primitives (Reuse, Adapt via LoRA, New, Skip), learned via a single-path supernet with task-similarity-guided hierarchical sampling (HEE-NAS) and a compute-aware evolutionary search. The pipeline is described in enough detail (Secs. 3.2-3.5) to be reproducible, and code is promised.

Comprehensive and mostly fair empirical evaluation: two challenging, imbalanced benchmarks (MTIL, VDD), two backbone scales (ViT-Base, DEiT-Tiny) plus CLIP ViT-B, three seeds, task-order robustness (Table 10), placement ablations (Table 8), HEE vs. uniform sampling ablation (Table 9), hyperparameter sensitivity (Fig. 10), and a smaller-model task-ID variant (Tables 15-16).

Strong main results: CHEEM closely approaches full fine-tuning upper bounds (e.g., 86.7% vs. 88.7% on VDD with ViT-Base; 76.18% vs. 76.21% for DEiT-Tiny) and clearly outperforms prompting baselines, while allocating lower FLOPs to easier tasks (Table 6) — supporting the task-difficulty-awareness claim.

The supplementary addresses a potential fairness concern: the large gap of L2P/CODA-P/DualPrompt is attributed to local-vs-global argmax, backed by both an empirical check (Table 19, giving baselines task IDs) and a stylized theoretical analysis (Sec. I). The component-placement study (Table 20) also provides an empirical basis for choosing MLPDown/projection layers.

Honest ablations: the comparison against LoRA-CL (a special case of CHEEM without NAS) quantifies the actual benefit of the search, and the uniform-sampling variant showing comparable accuracy (Table 9) is candidly discussed.
weaknesses: Marginal benefit over the simplest strong baseline on strong backbones: on ViT-Base, CHEEM improves over LoRA-CL by only ~1 point (85.9 vs. 84.7 MTIL; 86.7 vs. 86.0 VDD) at similar FLOPs. More concerning, with CLIP ViT-B (Tables 13-14) CHEEM is actually below LoRA-CL on accuracy (86.4 vs. 86.8 MTIL; 84.5 vs. 85.8 VDD), winning only on FLOPs. This tempers the generality of the claim that structural NAS is broadly necessary.

Incremental novelty relative to L2G [32], which already introduced reuse/adapt/new structural learning for continual learning; the main deltas are the ViT/LoRA instantiation, the Skip operation, SPOS-based training, and the task-similarity-guided sampling. The HEE sampling itself is a heuristic with several hyperparameters (epsilon_1, epsilon_2, tau, top-k) whose tuning burden is nontrivial despite the ablations.

The proposed Figure-of-Merit (Eqn. 6) is a self-referential metric co-designed with the method: it normalizes both accuracy gap and FLOPs against a chosen upper bound and baseline, and its ratio form yields very large, hard-to-interpret values (e.g., 2811 for CODA-P on VDD/DEiT-Tiny) driven by denominator effects rather than practically meaningful differences. Raw metrics are reported, but headline claims lean on FoM.

Like S-Prompts, CHEEM relies on external task-centroid memory and explicit task-ID inference at test time, plus an additional forward pass (roughly doubling FLOPs, Tables 2-3). While the task-ID assumption is disclosed and increasingly common, this is a weaker setting than exemplar-free methods that require no task inference, and the paper's framing of 'beating prompting methods' partly reflects this setting difference (partially mitigated by Table 19).

The 'theoretical justification' in Sec. I is a stylized Gaussian-logit argument with independence assumptions; it motivates but does not rigorously establish the local/global argmax discrepancy for trained networks.

Evaluation breadth is limited to two related multi-domain benchmarks; no comparison on standard (if less realistic) benchmarks such as ImageNet-R split, which limits cross-paper comparability, and no analysis of behavior with a very large number of tasks where supernet/sampling costs and memory grow with t.

Presentation issues: some results are inconsistent across text/tables (e.g., CHEEM 85.88 vs. 85.9 avg acc; Moal/MoAL naming), Figs. 3b/3c architecture diagrams are dense and hard to parse, and Sec. J's placement selection mixes transferability and forgetting criteria in a somewhat ad hoc way.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation: two challenging, imbalanced benchmarks (MTIL, VDD), two backbone scales (ViT-Base, DEiT-Tiny) plus CLIP ViT-B, three seeds, and a broad baseline set including recent PEFT-CL methods (DIKI, MoAL, Tuna) and task-to-task fine-tuning upper bounds.

Performance is convincingly close to the full fine-tuning upper bound (e.g., 86.7 vs 88.7 on VDD for ViT-Base; 76.18 vs 76.21 for DEiT-Tiny) with substantially lower FLOPs than LoRA-CL, and results are robust to task order (Table 10).

Substantial ablation coverage: CHEEM placement (MLPDown vs attention projection, Table 8), HEE vs uniform sampling (Table 9), exploration probability and tolerance threshold sensitivity (Fig. 10), lightweight task-ID backbones (Tables 15-16), and component-wise identification of where to place the memory (Table 20).
The supplementary analysis of local vs. global argmax (Sec. I, Table 19) is a useful diagnostic that explains why prompting baselines collapse on imbalanced benchmarks.
The learned per-task architectures (Figs. 3, 6, 7) qualitatively support the task-difficulty-aware compute claim, e.g., skipping MLPs for MNIST/EuroSAT.
weaknesses: The method fundamentally relies on task-ID inference via an external centroid memory adopted from prior art (S-Prompts [60]), yet the headline comparisons include many task-agnostic prompting methods (L2P, DualPrompt, CODA-P). Table 19 shows these methods reach ~80-84% under local argmax with a task ID, so much of the reported gap reflects head-design assumptions rather than the proposed internal memory mechanism, making the 'state-of-the-art, outperforming prior art by a large margin' framing partly an apples-to-oranges comparison.

Limited novelty over existing components: the four-operation reuse/adapt/new/skip design closely follows L2G [32] (acknowledged), the supernet training is SPOS [19], the search is regularized evolution [49], the external memory is S-Prompts [60]; the main new element is the hierarchical CLS-similarity-based sampling, whose benefit is modest (Table 9 shows uniform sampling achieves on-par or higher accuracy, e.g., 75.05 vs 74.51 for DEiT-Tiny, and the parameter savings are the main advantage).

The self-proposed Figure-of-Merit (FoM, Eqn. 6) is a relative, pairwise metric dependent on the chosen upper bound and FLOPs accounting; it is non-standard and some headline claims rest on it rather than on standard metrics.

On the strongest backbone (CLIP ViT-B, Table 13), LoRA-CL—a 'special case' of CHEEM without NAS—actually slightly outperforms CHEEM (86.8 vs 86.4 on MTIL), tempering the claimed benefit of the full NAS machinery; the NAS advantage appears mainly for weaker backbones.

Pipeline complexity is significant: supernet training + evolutionary search + retraining with several hand-tuned hyperparameters (ε1, ε2, τ, top-k, mutation rate), and per-task training time is ~4x that of S-Prompts/DIKI/LoRA-CL (Table 7).
The VDD benchmark is reconstructed from original images rather than the released low-resolution version, complicating direct comparability with prior VDD results.
Theoretical analysis in Sec. I is largely qualitative and rests on strong simplifications (independent Gaussian logits), providing intuition rather than falsifiable predictions.

strengths: Comprehensive and convincing empirical evaluation: CHEEM is tested on two challenging, imbalanced benchmarks (MTIL and VDD) with both ViT-Base and DEiT-Tiny, three random seeds, and full per-task results reported in the appendix (Tables 11-12), allowing verification of headline numbers rather than only aggregates.

The core idea of a task-difficulty/synergy-aware dynamic backbone via four operations (Reuse, Adapt, New, Skip) is well-motivated and clearly distinguishes the work from prompting-based (frozen backbone) and uniform parameter-tuning (all layers adapted) approaches; qualitative learned architectures (Figs. 3, 6-9) plausibly correlate with task complexity (e.g., skipping 8 MLP blocks for MNIST).

CHEEM closely approaches the full fine-tuning upper bound (e.g., 86.7% vs 88.7% on VDD with ViT-Base; 76.18% vs 76.21% for DEiT-Tiny), while reducing compute relative to LoRA-CL, and shows robustness to task ordering (Table 10) and generalization to CLIP backbones (Tables 13-14).

Thorough ablation studies covering placement (MLPDown vs Attn Proj, Table 20), HEE vs uniform sampling (Table 9), exploration probabilities and tolerance thresholds (Fig. 10), task-ID inference with lightweight backbones (Tables 15-16), and training overhead (Table 7), which collectively support the design choices and practicality.

The identification of the local vs. global argmax discrepancy in task-agnostic heads is a useful empirical observation explaining why several popular prompting methods fail on imbalanced benchmarks, backed by controlled experiments (Table 19) and a supplementary analysis.
Reproducibility is supported: code is released, implementation details are extensive (optimizer, epochs, epsilon/tau settings, checkpoints, splits), and the paper is clearly written.
weaknesses: The method is a fairly incremental extension of prior continual structure-learning work, most notably L2G [32] (which already used differentiable search over reuse/adapt/new operations) and PathNet/SPOS-style NAS; the paper is candid about this, and the principal novelty reduces to (i) the ViT/MLPDown-Projection instantiation, (ii) the Skip operation, and (iii) the HEE similarity-guided sampling. The demonstrated benefit of HEE over uniform sampling is on-par accuracy with fewer added parameters, which is modest.

Heavy reliance on a self-introduced Figure-of-Merit (FoM) metric for headline claims. FoM is non-standard, anchored to an upper bound, and its magnitude can be inflated by baseline failures rather than method strengths (e.g., FoM of 678.9 for EWC and 2811.3 for CODA-P on VDD with DEiT-Tiny simply reflect catastrophic baseline collapse, which makes the table's interpretation awkward). Standard metrics in Tables 4-5 tell a less dramatic story: on ViT-Base, CHEEM's accuracy advantage over LoRA-CL is about 1.2 points (85.9 vs 84.7 on MTIL; 86.7 vs 86.0 on VDD), and on CLIP ViT-B/16 CHEEM actually underperforms LoRA-CL (86.4 vs 86.8 on MTIL; 84.5 vs 85.8 on VDD).

The method requires task-specific heads plus an external task-centroid memory for task-ID inference (borrowed from S-Prompts [60]), essentially the domain-incremental decomposition strategy. This is a defensible design and is shared with some baselines, but it sidesteps part of the difficulty that class-incremental, task-agnostic methods must face, so claims of solving ExfCCL should be tempered; the supplementary 'theoretical analysis' (Sec. I) is stylized and largely informal, adding limited technical depth.

Baseline performance on these benchmarks appears surprisingly low for prompt-based methods (e.g., L2P at 26.6% and CODA-P at 40.2% on MTIL ViT-Base, far below commonly reported behavior), which the authors attribute to head-design and data-imbalance issues; while the local-argmax experiment (Table 19) is a useful diagnostic, several baselines were re-implemented by the authors and verification against published numbers is not provided, raising a fairness concern for the FoM comparisons.

The pipeline has multiple tuned hyperparameters (epsilon_1, epsilon_2, tau, top-k, mutation rate, similarity normalization) whose selection is benchmark-dependent; sensitivity is studied, but the extra machinery adds complexity, and FLOPs nearly double due to the extra forward pass for task-ID inference unless a second lightweight model is used (the CHEEMlite variant).

FLOPs comparisons are inference-only; training cost of CHEEM (1.45h vs 0.38-1.26h per task in Table 7) is higher than most baselines, which somewhat offsets the efficiency narrative, though the authors report this transparently.
